title: Optimize auto-tuner incident: lessons learned and safe-apply playbook
creator: Priya Desai
description: Unplanned production regression triggered by the Optimize service's automatic configuration apply path. During a routine autotune cycle the optimizer ramped batching window and reduced prefix caching aggressiveness which produced KV cache thrash on a small but high-latency customer cohort. The result was elevated tail latency, cascading queueing on some dedicated pools, increased token re-generation, and a measurable cost surge due to fallbacks to larger model variants and repeated retries. This ticket captures a concise postmortem, immediate mitigations, and a prescriptive safe-apply playbook to prevent recurrence.
timeline: 2026-02-24T02:10Z - Autotuner scheduled a global apply after completing offline recommendations
2026-02-24T02:12Z - Canary rollout (2% traffic) passed synthetic checks; global gating allowed apply
2026-02-24T02:18Z - Metrics show rising p99 latency for two dedicated pools serving long-session chat flows
2026-02-24T02:26Z - Error rate climb triggered automated throttles but not rollback; on-call alerted
2026-02-24T02:40Z - Manual intervention initiated: reduce request rate and enable emergency fallback configs
2026-02-24T03:05Z - Full rollback to previous config completed; latency and error rates normalized by 03:20Z
root_cause: The autotuner produced a coupled configuration change: increasing batching window while lowering cache retention TTL. On long-tail sessions this created frequent KV cache misses and larger batches with higher end-to-end service time. The combined effect exceeded assumptions in the canary gating logic which only evaluated mean latency and synthetic traffic patterns, missing the real-world heavy-tailed session distribution.
contributing_factors: Canary gating evaluated synthetic load with limited session length variance (missed long-tail behavior)
Autotuner applies were global without progressive regional ramp-down when higher variance observed
No hard cost guardrail in apply path—optimizer could recommend config that increases cost transiently
Lack of an explicit cache-thrashing detector in tuning analysis
Runbook rollback automation required manual confirmation under current thresholds
immediate_mitigations: Temporarily disable autotune global applies for Optimize until safety controls are in place
Elevate canary to include synthetic long-session traces representative of tail traffic
Apply emergency rate-limiting on affected dedicated pools to prevent queue spiral
Notify impacted customers and open follow-up support tickets where SLA breach occurred
rollback_criteria: p99 latency increase > 40% over baseline for > 5 minutes
error rate (5xx) increase > 2x baseline for > 3 minutes
cost per token > 1.5x baseline for 15 minutes attributable to model fallbacks
more than 3 instances in a pool showing sustained queue length growth for 10 minutes
safety_playbook_steps: Pre-apply: run offline simulation that injects long-session traces and measure KV miss amplification
Pre-apply: compute delta in expected cost and abort if predicted cost > configured guardrail
Canary: start at 0.5% traffic and include at least one dedicated pool region with long-tail workloads
Observability: require p50/p90/p99 and cache hit ratio trending checks, plus a KV-thrash signal
Canary gating: block progressive rollout if any rollback_criteria condition is met during canary
Progressive rollout: 0.5% -> 2% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with minimum dwell time of 15 minutes and automatic rollback hooks
Post-apply: schedule a 24h cost and latency audit with automated report to owners
Human-in-loop: any canary alert triggers on-call review within 3 minutes and automatic pause of rollout until acknowledged
monitoring_alert_rules: optimize.autotuner.p99_latency.spike: p99 latency increase > 40% vs baseline for 5m
postmortem_summary: The incident was caused by unexpected interaction between batching and cache TTL recommendations produced by the optimizer. Canary validation did not capture long-session behavior, allowing a hazardous global apply. Root causes include insufficient canary traffic diversity, lack of cost guardrails, and missing cache-thrash detection. The team rolled back the change within 30 minutes; customers with long sessions experienced elevated latency and a small number of SLA misses. No customer data was exposed.
